entries.clue: Section of Hawkwind EP thrills thoroughly (2,5)

indicatorNotes.Section of: a section is a slice of the words that follow

blocks.note: hawkwIND EP THrills, running across three words

annotation.surface: A music reviewer praising part of a record by the rock band Hawkwind.
annotation.walkthrough: Hawkwind is a British space-rock band, so the surface reads naturally as a review; 'thoroughly' looks like praise for the EP but is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain adverbial synonym: a subject studied with full, detailed attention is covered thoroughly.

entries.clue: Make better, mostly unscripted performance (6)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word, not all of it: the last letter goes

annotation.surface: Advice that improvised theatre could be made better.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is at the end; 'Make better' is the wordplay, which is only trimmed by one letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A clipped form of improvisation: comedy or theatre made up on the spot, with no script.

entries.clue: Shortage of diamonds on ground (6)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the next

annotation.surface: A remark that few diamonds are found on the ground.
annotation.walkthrough: D for diamonds is the card-suit abbreviation, as in bridge notation.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns mean too little of something, as in a lack of food or jobs.

entries.clue: Pity person’s corrupt tendency (10)

indicatorNotes.corrupt: corrupted letters are spoiled out of their proper order

annotation.surface: A judgement that someone's leaning towards corruption is to be pitied.
annotation.walkthrough: Read the ’s as 'is': the fodder is corrupt, which gives a tendency. 'Corrupt' pretends to be an adjective describing the tendency.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name an inclination to behave a certain way, as in a leaning towards laziness.

entries.clue: Animal that wades in cool Italian river (5)

annotation.surface: A picture of a large animal wading in a refreshing Italian river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cool' looks like the temperature of the water, but it means fashionable.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the hippopotamus, whose name means river horse, spends its days wading and wallowing.

entries.clue: Gave energy to captive soldier, English revolutionary (7)

blocks.note: a red is a communist revolutionary

annotation.surface: Someone encouraging a captured soldier who happens to be an English rebel.
annotation.walkthrough: Three standard abbreviations in a row; the surface reads as one captive rather than three pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: a battery or engine supplied a machine with its driving force.

entries.clue: Print media admitting certain stresses (9)

indicatorNotes.admitting: to admit is to let in, so the first piece holds the second

annotation.surface: A newspaper story conceding that some tensions exist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Admitting' pretends the papers are confessing something, but it means taking in.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain plural-noun synonym: the strains and demands of work or life.

entries.clue: Broad gets a run in cricket (4)

blocks.note: an adjective for something of great width
the extra run awarded when a ball is bowled out of the batter's reach

annotation.surface: A report that Stuart Broad, the England fast bowler, has scored a run.
annotation.walkthrough: Stuart Broad is a famous English cricketer, so the capital B hides a plain adjective. In cricket a wide is penalised by awarding the batting side a run.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for broad, and the cricket term for the penalty run given for a ball bowled too far from the batter.

entries.clue: Royal Artillery battalion ultimately fires rifles (8)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately = in the end, so take the last letter

blocks.note: to sack = to fire from a job

annotation.surface: An army scene: gunners from the Royal Artillery firing their rifles.
annotation.walkthrough: The military surface makes 'fires' and 'rifles' look like shooting, but 'fires' means dismisses and 'rifles' is a verb meaning searches through.
annotation.definitionFit: The verb sense of rifles: to search a place roughly, stealing as you go.

entries.clue: Command party friend hosts at home (8)

indicatorNotes.hosts: a host holds guests inside, so MATE holds IN

annotation.surface: An order to a party-going friend who is entertaining at their own house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Command' looks like a noun heading the clue but works as a verb, as when a castle commands a valley.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to have control over, or to tower over a view or position.

entries.clue: Musical instrument, or instruction for how to play it (5)

annotation.definition2: instruction for how to play it

blocks.note: the keyboard instrument with hammers and strings

blocks.clueFragment: instruction for how to play it
blocks.note: the Italian score marking, written p, telling the player to play softly

annotation.surface: A playful note that one word names an instrument and tells you how to play it.
annotation.walkthrough: The instrument's full name, pianoforte, means soft-loud, so its short name is the same word as the direction to play quietly.
annotation.definitionFit: The keyboard instrument by name, and the Italian dynamic marking for soft playing.

entries.clue: E.g. Picaroon in terrible dump? Yes and no (9)

indicatorNotes.terrible: the letters are in a terrible state, badly mixed

annotation.surface: The setter, Picaroon, stuck in a dreadful dump, and not sure whether that is true.
annotation.walkthrough: Picaroon is this puzzle's setter, and like all Guardian setters writes under an assumed name. The fodder is DUMP, YES and NO; 'and' is surface glue.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Picaroon is the setter's crossword pen name, not their real one.

entries.clue: Where solar panels are installed for free (2,3,5)

blocks.note: a literal location: up on the roof of a home
an idiom for something paid for by the establishment, like a free drink in a bar

annotation.surface: A promise that solar panels will be fitted at no charge.
annotation.walkthrough: The first definition is literal, the second idiomatic, and the surface fuses them into one sales pitch.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal place for rooftop panels, and the idiom for a drink or meal the establishment gives away.

entries.clue: Starts to plan attack with knight, or other chess piece (4)

indicatorNotes.Starts to: the starts of the next words are their first letters

blocks.note: first letters of Plan Attack With

annotation.surface: Chess advice: begin your attack with a knight, or with some other piece.
annotation.walkthrough: In chess notation the knight is N, since K is taken by the king. 'With' is part of the initials, not a link.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the humblest chess piece, other than the knight the wordplay has just used.

entries.clue: Wind player with nothing on, caught by strings player (10)

indicatorNotes.caught by: to be caught by someone is to be held in their hands

blocks.note: a bassist plays the double bass or bass guitar

annotation.surface: A naked woodwind player being grabbed by a musician from the string section.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With nothing on' paints nudity but is two pieces that the strings player swallows.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the bassoon is a woodwind instrument, so its player is a wind player.

entries.clue: Big shop possibly making Starmer puke (11)

indicatorNotes.possibly: the letters could possibly be arranged another way

annotation.surface: A large shop that might make Keir Starmer, the UK Labour leader, throw up.
annotation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer is a British Labour politician and Prime Minister; his name supplies seven of the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: a large self-service store selling food and household goods.

entries.clue: Jumpers turned up by Leicester’s number one fans (9)

indicatorNotes.turned: turned round, so UP runs backwards
indicatorNotes.number one: Leicester's number one is its first letter

annotation.surface: Football supporters of Leicester City arriving in woolly sweaters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as 'arrived', but UP is the fodder and 'turned' reverses it. Jumper is British for a sweater, not someone who jumps.
annotation.definitionFit: A British synonym: jumpers and pullovers are both knitted sweaters pulled on over the head.

entries.clue: Account by clergyman is error-free (8)

blocks.note: AC = account, as on a bank statement
a curate is an assistant priest; 'by' places it beside AC

annotation.surface: A vicar's record of events vouched for as correct.
annotation.walkthrough: A curate is a junior clergyman in the Church of England, assisting a vicar or rector.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain adjective synonym: correct in every detail, with no mistakes.

entries.clue: Stimulating drug reduced – a kind of blow (8)

annotation.surface: A news line about a lowered dose of stimulant being a blow to someone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A kind of blow' could suggest drugs slang, but it is a punch.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a boxing punch thrown upward at the chin.

entries.clue: City is walling off street for financiers etc.? (11)

indicatorNotes.walling off: IS builds a wall round ST, enclosing it

blocks.note: a capital is a chief city

annotation.surface: The City of London fencing off a street for its bankers.
annotation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, which makes the surface about banking. The question mark flags that financiers are only one kind of capitalist.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: financiers put money to work for profit, one group among investors and business owners.

entries.clue: Aircraft heads for Greece’s largest island, doing extra refuelling (6)

indicatorNotes.heads for: the head of each word is its first letter

blocks.clueFragment: Greece’s largest island, doing extra refuelling
blocks.note: first letters of Greece's Largest Island Doing Extra Refuelling

annotation.surface: A plane flying to Crete, Greece's biggest island, making an extra fuel stop.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is that a glider has no engine and never refuels at all.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: an engineless craft that flies on rising air.

entries.clue: English King Lear who wrote nonsense (6)

blocks.note: the royal name shared by eight kings of England
the first name of the Victorian nonsense poet behind 'The Owl and the Pussy-Cat'

annotation.surface: King Lear, Shakespeare's monarch, pictured as the author of nonsense.
annotation.walkthrough: 'King Lear' runs together as Shakespeare's play, but the break falls between them: King ends one definition and Lear starts the other.
annotation.definitionFit: A name shared by eight English kings and by the nonsense poet Lear.

entries.clue: Guardian compilers and our boss getting exploited (4)

blocks.note: the setters of this Guardian puzzle, speaking of themselves
ed = editor, the boss of a newspaper

annotation.surface: A complaint from Guardian setters that they and their editor are being taken advantage of.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter speaks from inside the paper, so the surface is a staff grumble; 'and' simply joins the two pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the passive: taken advantage of by someone.

entries.clue: Prisoner provoked people on-line, getting restrained (10)

blocks.note: a con = a convict, a prisoner
to troll is to provoke people on the internet

annotation.surface: An inmate who baited people on the internet ending up locked down.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is one internet troll's comeuppance; each half is a plain synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: held in check, kept within limits.

entries.clue: Teacher’s disapproving word over losing heart (5)

indicatorNotes.losing heart: the heart of a word is its middle, which goes

blocks.note: tut is the click of disapproval

annotation.surface: A teacher tutting at a pupil who has given up.
annotation.walkthrough: Read the ’s as 'is'. 'Over' looks like the down-clue placement word, but it is the word that loses its heart.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who teaches, usually one pupil or a small group.

entries.clue: City with famous tower – Paris strangely not right (4)

indicatorNotes.not right: R for right is taken away

annotation.surface: Paris has a famous tower, yet somehow it is the wrong city.
annotation.walkthrough: The Eiffel Tower points to Paris, which is the fodder; the city meant has a different famous tower.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the Tuscan city known worldwide for its leaning bell tower.

entries.clue: Wren perhaps in the Arctic, oddly (9)

indicatorNotes.oddly: the letters are arranged oddly, strangely

annotation.surface: A small bird, a wren, turning up strangely in the Arctic.
annotation.walkthrough: Sir Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral in London. 'Oddly' wants to mean the odd letters, but those do not give the answer; here it means strangely.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'perhaps': Christopher Wren designed buildings, most famously St Paul's.

entries.clue: Golf, then hotel, then this part of Asia (5)

annotation.definition: Golf, then hotel, then this part of Asia

blocks.note: the surface reads as a holiday itinerary; the setter means the radio alphabet words for G and H
the next word in that alphabet, for I, is also the name of a South Asian country

annotation.surface: A travel itinerary: a golf trip, a hotel stay, then a country in Asia.
annotation.walkthrough: Golf and Hotel are the NATO phonetic alphabet words for G and H; the next letter's word is India, which is also in Asia.
annotation.definitionFit: The country is a part of Asia, and its name is the phonetic-alphabet word that follows Golf and Hotel.

entries.clue: Stitches up parent’s pants (7)

indicatorNotes.pants: British slang for rubbish: the letters are in a bad state

annotation.surface: Someone sewing up a parent's trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain pants means underpants, and as slang 'pants' means rubbish, which makes it a mixing signal. 'Stitches up' is British slang for frames.
annotation.definitionFit: A British slang sense: to stitch someone up is to frame or trick them into trouble.

entries.clue: Withdrew sappers in need of a rest (7)

blocks.note: RE = Royal Engineers, whose soldiers are called sappers
tired = in need of a rest

annotation.surface: Exhausted army engineers pulling back from the front.
annotation.walkthrough: Sappers are the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps.
annotation.definitionFit: A past-tense synonym: pulled back, as an army does from a position or a person does to bed.
